title: Deterministic Verification and a Single-Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation reused for both conditions) we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit a single automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered sim‑to‑real/production-like confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition actually run. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle (preregistration SHA-256: 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate operator intent into device CLI sequences for NetOps automation. Stochastic generation can produce syntax errors, ordering mistakes, and vendor-specific subtleties that pose operational risk. A common mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern that accepts only candidates passing a deterministic validator or attempts bounded automated repair. Prior surveys and empirical studies document feasibility of LLM draft configurations and motivate deterministic validators, but the marginal effect of inserting a validator+single repair on identical model outputs remains unclear when generation is held fixed. Our preregistered experiment isolates that marginal effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent we produced exactly one LLM candidate and compared accepting that candidate (baseline) to submitting it to a deterministic validator and allowing up to one automated repair (guarded). The research question is: when the same natural-language intent is realized by an identical LLM-generated candidate, how large is the paired difference in verifier-confirmed intent-satisfaction between accepting the candidate and applying a deterministic validator plus one automated repair in a constrained synthetic/emulation partition? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired, shared-candidate experiment (N_pairs = 250) that quantifies the verifier+single-repair marginal effect with full execution accounting; (2) artifact-grounded numeric bounds on the maximum verifier-detected improvement under the executed conditions; and (3) an analysis of failure modes, power consequences, and reproducibility artifacts.
sections.related_work: Existing work documents two motivating facts: (a) LLMs can produce usable draft network configurations in controlled setups, but often require verification or human oversight; and (b) deterministic verification and generate–verify–repair architectures reduce mechanically checkable defects (syntax, ordering, local-policy violations) though deeper semantic correctness and cross-vendor issues remain challenging. Prior tool and technique surveys (network-configuration verification, Batfish/plankton-like approaches, and LLM-for-NetOps reviews) establish the validation primitives used in this study and motivate paired generate–validate evaluations. Security analyses of prompt-injection and retrieval-based threats emphasize the need for filtering and validation layers but show adaptive adversaries remain an open problem. Our study differs by (i) using a preregistered paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics to isolate the validator/repair marginal effect on identical candidates, (ii) reconciling provider-call accounting at stage level (shared initial generation vs repair), and (iii) archiving complete validator traces and reconciliation artifacts for audit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and specified a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration froze the single-repair policy, exclusion rules, and the analysis plan (exact McNemar two-sided and paired-bootstrap percentile CIs). The preregistration artifact SHA-256 is provided in the Disclosure.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution accounting. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one initial model-generation call was produced per intent and that same generated candidate was reused for both episodes (baseline and guarded); no independent first-pass generation per condition was performed. Provider-call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251, with stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}. Those stage counts reflect 250 shared initial generations plus a single repair invocation exercised during the run.

Task generation, model, validator, and repair policy. A deterministic task generator produced 250 constrained intent tasks; each payload encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). The declared model for all initial generations was gpt-5-mini. The guarded pipeline applied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, implementing full_intent_constraint_validation (CLI parsing, required_sequence ordering, workflow constraints, and final_state snapshot comparison). If the validator returned valid = false the pipeline permitted up to one automated, template-driven repair (deterministic syntactic and ordering fixes only) and re-submitted the repaired candidate once.

Inclusion, contamination, and missingness rules. The preregistered exclusions removed items that failed vendor-parsers preventing verification or contained credential-like tokens or denylist hits. Contamination detectors flagged instruction-like embedded tokens. The primary analysis excludes flagged items by design; sensitivity analyses were specified. In the executed confirmatory partition no episodes were excluded or flagged.

Analysis procedures. The primary test is the exact two-sided McNemar on paired binary outcomes. We also computed a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the guarded − baseline paired difference using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The analysis executor and raw analysis artifacts are archived.
sections.results:
Execution summary. The run completed planned_episode_count = 500, completed_episode_count = 500, complete_pair_count = 250, and model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial-generation + 1 repair). No episodes were excluded; contamination detectors flagged zero confirmatory episodes.

Primary outcomes. Validator-scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.004 (0.4 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the guarded − baseline difference = [0.0, 0.012] (i.e., 0.0–1.2 percentage points). The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair; repair-conversion rate in the confirmatory partition = 1/250 = 0.004 (0.4%). Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count and required_command_count matching task-required sequences for passed episodes (examples archived).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. Under the executed, tightly constrained synthetic/emulation partition and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the marginal verifier-detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus one automated repair was small: initial gpt-5-mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the single repair converted the sole failing candidate. The paired-bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) bounds the maximum verifier-detected improvement under these conditions.

Why the effect is small. Artifact-grounded factors explain the near-null marginal gain: (1) the deterministic task generator produced constrained, low-ambiguity intents and explicit allowed_touched_fields that reduced generation ambiguity; (2) gpt-5-mini produced highly consistent, syntactically well-formed outputs for these constrained prompts; and (3) the deterministic validator measured mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, snapshot final_state) but not broader runtime or behavioral correctness.

Power and preregistration assumptions. The preregistration power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 to detect a 15 percentage-point effect with N_pairs = 250. The realized baseline pass rate (0.996) exceeded that assumption substantially, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements; thus the reported CI and upper bound on possible benefit are the most informative outputs under the actual data.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: sensitivity to prompt templates, the single-repair policy, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. Construct validity: the validator captures mechanically checkable correctness but not live protocol behavior. External validity: results are limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed. Security: adaptive prompt-injection and retrieval-based attacks were not evaluated.

Operational implications and caution. These results do not imply validators or repairs are unnecessary in practice. In broader, heterogeneous, or adversarial environments validators that check additional properties or multi‑iteration repairs could provide larger benefits. The evidence here quantifies the marginal verifier-detected improvement only for the constrained experimental scope executed.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment with shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the marginal verifier-detected effect of a deterministic validator plus one automated repair on identical LLM-generated candidates. In 250 constrained synthetic intents gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the single permitted repair converted the lone failing candidate. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). The preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition actually run. Broader production, adversarial, multi-model, and multi‑iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All run artifacts and analysis manifests are archived in the study evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: after an autonomy lock required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, prompt preservation, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre-lock infrastructure development only.

Models, tools, and permitted framework: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution used a guarded generate–verify–repair flow permitting at most one automated repair per episode as specified in the preregistration. Execution accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Preregistration and immutable master prompt references (archived): preregistration study id = study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 (preregistration SHA-256: 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede). Immutable master prompt used to initiate the autonomous run: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The full execution and analysis evidence bundle (artifact manifest available) contains the execution manifest, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, deterministic reconciliation, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production-like partitions were not executed.
Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, final_state snapshot) but did not measure runtime protocol behavior or emergent cross-device effects.
Single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repairs or human-in-the-loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adaptive adversarial and retrieval-based attacks, and broader production heterogeneity, were not exercised and remain open threats.
